web_evidence.title: For Whom the Bell Tolls | Book by Ernest Hemingway | Official Publisher Page
web_evidence.note: Scribner's authorized Chapter One excerpt sustains external past-tense narration of Robert Jordan and the old man as 'he,' independently corroborating the quote evidence.

web_evidence.title: For Whom the Bell Tolls: Themes, Techniques, and Analysis
web_evidence.note: Hemingway scholar Mark Cirino explicitly identifies a third-person, omniscient narrator and explains that the narration can leave Jordan to follow El Sordo and Andrés.

web_evidence.title: “That Was Thinking in Spanish”: Translated Style and Interlingual Strangeness in Hemingway
web_evidence.note: This scholarly essay states that the book is narrated in third person and explains that its narration often blends with Robert Jordan's inner thoughts, resolving apparent first-person passages as interior monologue.

web_evidence.title: AMST 246 - Lecture 17 - Hemingway's For Whom the Bell Tolls, Part II
web_evidence.note: The Yale lecture explicitly identifies an apparent narrative 'you' as Robert Jordan addressing himself and notes the passage's switch back to third person.

web_evidence.title: For Whom The Bell Tolls: Key Facts
web_evidence.note: The guide explicitly identifies an anonymous third-person narrator, usually restricted to Robert Jordan's perceptions but occasionally commenting on other action.

person_note: The controlling narrator is nonparticipating and third person. Multiple substantial quotes narrate Robert Jordan externally as 'he,' while the authorized opening and several structural sources independently confirm a third-person narrator that can move among characters. The conspicuous first- and second-person event excerpts are local direct thought or self-address by Robert Jordan or Anselmo; Yale and the scholarly style analysis specifically document this movement between Jordan's self-directed 'you' and third-person framing. Dialogue, maxims, and verse likewise do not alter the base person. No source indicates sustained first- or second-person base sections, so these local voice changes do not warrant ALTERNATING. The remaining uncertainty is limited to attribution of a few clipped quotes, not the book-level classification.
